extracted.intended_audience: users/programmers of the PARI/GP computer algebra system (mathematicians, number_theorists, scientists writing gp scripts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and usage rules for entering expressions, types, operators, variables, and data structures in the PARI/GP interactive language (gp). Covers input syntax, semantics, performance caveats and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line continuation with backslash
rubrics_metrics.description: A backslash \ immediately followed by a newline causes gp to ignore that newline, so the token you will write on the next line is the physical continuation of what you have just written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ? 3 + \ (newline) 4 instead of typing 3 + 4. The backslash must be immediately followed by a newline (apart from ignored whitespace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Line continuation after '='
rubrics_metrics.description: Since an equal sign can never end a valid expression, gp disregards a newline immediately following an '='.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when defining a user function: ? a = (newline) 123 produces %1 = 123.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-line commands with braces
rubrics_metrics.description: An opening brace { signals a multi-line command; newlines are ignored until the matching } is typed. Braces do not nest and inside { } all input lines are concatenated (newlines suppressed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrictions: braces do not nest; never split an identifier across lines inside braces. Newlines should occur after semicolon, comma or operator. Anti-pattern: writing { a = b (newline) b = c } becomes a=bb=c (wrong). Always terminate statements with semicolons inside braces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types t_INT, t_REAL, etc. provided for convenience not speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Several higher-level PARI types (t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, t_PADIC, t_QUAD, t_POLMOD, t_RFRAC) are provided for convenience but are not always the most efficient representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each elementary operation on these types often performs reductions (gcd, modulo, etc.) which can be wasteful in large recursive computations; consider using libpari or integer/homomorphic methods for performance-critical code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integer input rules (t_INT)
rubrics_metrics.description: After an optional leading + or -, type decimal digits only (no decimal point) to input an integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hexadecimal: prefix 0x (digits a..f in either case). Binary: prefix 0b. Examples: ? 1234567, ? -3, ? 0xF -> 15, ? 0b010101 -> 21. Beware that '1.' is not an integer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real number input and internal precision (t_REAL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real numbers (t_REAL) are entered with a decimal point (or scientific notation) and carry an internal precision (accuracy) determined by input digits and the default realprecision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trailing zeroes are significant for internal precision (e.g., 2.0...0 can give very high internal precision). Scientific notation with E/e allowed (6.02E23, 1e-5). 0.E n yields a zero real with exponent n; 0. yields zero of default precision. Use realprecision (\p) or realbitprecision (\ps) to inspect/set default; in programs prefer localbitprec to adapt precision locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero real output format
rubrics_metrics.description: A zero real is printed in e format as 0.Exx where xx is the decimal exponent, allowing inspection of accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the integer part is not known exactly because exponent > precision, the real is printed in e format. This helps debug precision/accuracy issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: INTMODs: creation and cost (t_INTMOD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create residue class Mod(a,b) to represent integers in Z/bZ; internally operations use representatives in [0,b-1] and each elementary operation does a reduction modulo b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Mod(a,b) (not a % b). Member function x.mod returns modulus b. INTMODs are convenient but slower per operation than bare integers; still much faster than working with t_FRAC in some modular computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractions always reduced (t_FRAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: All rational numbers are automatically reduced to lowest terms; you cannot work with reducible fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Input n/m for rationals. Floating point division is not performed (no 3/2 -> 1.5). Rational arithmetic invokes gcds per operation—often slower; prefer cancelling denominators and integer arithmetic, homomorphic imaging, or t_INTMODs for modular needs. Examples show significant speed differences in polynomial operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite field elements (t_FFELT) construction and members
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ffinit to create the finite field and ffgen to create its generator; ffgen(T,'y) creates the generator y; finite field elements have member functions g.pol, g.p, g.f, g.mod.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ? T = ffinit(2,8); ? y = ffgen(T,'y); then y^8 yields a polynomial expression. The optional name parameter affects printing only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex numbers input (t_COMPLEX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enter complex numbers as x + I*y (capital I denotes sqrt(-1)); real and imaginary parts can be of several PARI types (t_INT, t_REAL, t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, t_PADIC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use I (not i). Components can be different PARI types as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-adic numbers input and caveats (t_PADIC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing O(p^k) yields a p-adic zero of accuracy k; to enter a general p-adic, give a rational/integer approximation plus O(p^k). p is not checked to be prime and results are undefined if p is composite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 2*7^(-1) + 3 + 4*7 + 2*7^2 + O(7^3) or 905/7 + O(7^3). Member functions a.mod (pk) and a.p (p). t_PADICs are convenient but slow per operation because pk updates and reductions occur; additions are particularly slow. For intensive iteration use Mod(1,2^20) or integers where appropriate for speed comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic numbers via quadgen (t_QUAD)
rubrics_metrics.description: quadgen(d) assigns the canonical generator w for the quadratic order of discriminant d (d non-square congruent to 0 or 1 mod 4); elements are entered as x + y*w with integers or rationals for x,y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: quadgen(d) prints as w regardless of variable name. Member functions: z.disc, real(z), imag(z). Beware two t_QUADs may print the same but be unequal; gp will refuse some mixed operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial mod objects (t_POLMOD) and variable consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Mod(x,y) to create polmods; each operation performs a reduction modulo y and polmods with modulus y are algebraic numbers when y is irreducible. Variables inside polmods are not free variables; internal operations require consistent main variable names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do NOT mix polmods that use different main variable names in internal operations as GP will not recognize Mod(y,y^2+1) as same as Mod(x,x^2+1). Polmods must use the same variable between polmods; see Section 2.5.3 on priority. Member functions: p.pol (representative) and p.mod (modulus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomials input rules and 'free variable' quote
rubrics_metrics.description: Type polynomials naturally but put * between coefficient and formal variable. To ensure a free variable, use 'x (quote) rather than x which may have an assigned value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1 + 2*x + 3*x^2 prints as polynomial unless x assigned; use 'x to get a free variable even if x has a value. Use Pol or Polrev constructors for efficiency (linear vs quadratic constructions). Avoid assigning values to polynomial variable names in serious programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomials printed univariate with decreasing degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynomials are printed as univariate polynomials with monomials sorted by decreasing degree; coefficients can themselves be polynomials (giving a multivariate interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (x+y+1)^2 prints as x^2 + (2*y + 2)*x + (y^2 + 2*y + 1) and is interpreted as a univariate polynomial in x with polynomial coefficients in y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series input and inexact-coefficient caveat (t_SER)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing O(X^k) yields an X-adic zero of accuracy k; to input a series give a polynomial/rational plus O(X^k). Power series with inexact coefficients can behave non-intuitively: inexact zeros may be counted as significant terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inverted with zero leading coefficient, gp may discard that coefficient and issue a warning to continue rather than raising exception. Examples show warnings: normalizing a series with 0 leading term. Insufficient series precision can lead to errors (division by zero), avoidable by better understanding of global precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational functions reduced to lowest terms (t_RFRAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: All rational functions are automatically reduced to lowest terms analogous to fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All remarks about t_FRAC (costs, gcds) apply here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary quadratic forms (t_QFR, t_QFI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary quadratic forms are input via Qfb(a,b,c); discriminant retrieved via poldisc; components obtained with Vec(q) or component(q,i). Imaginary forms (negative discriminant) are t_QFI; positive discriminant forms are t_QFR and may take an optional fourth real component related to regulator/distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qfbprimeform to create a prime form with given discriminant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vectors: syntax, indexing, slices and negative indices (t_VEC, t_COL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Row vectors use [a,b,c]; column vectors use transpose ~ or vectorv constructors. v[m] is m-th entry; v[i..j] returns slice; v[^i] returns vector with i-th entry removed. Negative indices count from end (-1 is last).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructors: vector(n,i,expr) for row vectors, vectorv for column. Vec/Col convert objects and Vecrev/Colrev reverse indexing. Example indexing: v = [1,2,3,4]; v[2..4] -> [2,3,4]; v[^3] removes 3rd element. Cannot assign to slices like v[i..j].

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector comprehensions and shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative set-notations [g(x) | x <- v, f(x)] and [x | x <- v, f(x)] are available as shortcuts for apply/select patterns and useful as vector constructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [ p | p <- primes(10), isprime(p+2) ] returns twin primes among first 10 primes; [ p^2 | p <- primes(10), p % 4 == 1 ] returns squares of primes ≡1 mod 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrices: syntax, indexing semantics and recursive access (t_MAT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matrices input row by row: [a,b; c,d]. Use commas for elements, semicolons for rows. M[i,j] refers to entry (i,j); M[i,] row; M[,j] column. Ranges and caret notations allowed for submatrices and slices; indexing is recursive allowing matrices of matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: M[1..2,2..3] returns submatrix; M[i..j,k] returns t_COL of column k between rows i..j. M[i] is meaningless (error). Assigning to M[i,] requires a t_VEC of right size. Recursive indexing like M[1,1][,3][4] is valid (identical to M[1,1][4,3]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix internal representation caveat (zero-column matrices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matrices are internally represented as a vector of columns. All matrices with 0 columns share the same internal object; it's impossible to represent matrices with zero columns and a nonzero number of rows distinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The empty matrix [;] is handled as having arbitrary number of rows as needed. Multiplying with an empty matrix interprets dimensions accordingly. Be cautious representing row vectors of column vectors vs true matrices—use Vec/Mat to convert representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists construction and element appending (t_LIST)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists can be created with List([ ... ]) or by creating empty List() then appending elements with listput(a, value). Elements accessed like vectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a = List(); listput(a,1); listput(a,2); a -> List([1,2]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strings (t_STR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strings are enclosed between double quotes "..."; Str() can convert objects to strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard string literal rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small vector internal type (t_VECSMALL)
rubrics_metrics.description: t_VECSMALL is an internal type used to efficiently code vectors of small integers (e.g., permutations); most gp functions will refuse to operate on these objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type is for internal efficiency only—do not rely on gp functions operating on t_VECSMALL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions and closures (t_CLOSURE) basic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions can be assigned to variables. Two basic equivalent forms: f = (x,y) -> x^2 + y^2 and f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Section 2.7 for detailed function construction and advanced use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error contexts (t_ERROR) and trapping with iferr
rubrics_metrics.description: An object of type t_ERROR is created when an error occurs; typically gp prints an error and aborts computation, entering the 'break loop'. Exceptions can be trapped using iferr to recover or inspect error context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: i = Mod(6,12); iferr(1/i, E, print(E)); 1 + 1 prints the error message then continues and returns 2. You can print component(E,1) to inspect error context, or rethrow using error(E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity objects (t_INFINITY)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only two objects +oo and -oo represent ±∞. They can be negated and compared to real numbers (t_INT, t_REAL, t_FRAC) but cannot participate in arithmetic computations (e.g., 1+oo is an error).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used primarily to encode infinite real intervals in functions like intnum or polrootsreal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator priorities, associativity and lvalue rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators have fixed priorities determining evaluation order; operators at same priority are left-associative unless noted; assignment operators are right-associative. An expression is an lvalue if something can be assigned to it; left-hand side of = must be an lvalue else error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a + b + c -> (a + b) + c (left-assoc). a = b = c -> a = (b = c) (right-assoc). If expression can't be parsed to make left side an lvalue, gp raises a syntax error (e.g., x+1=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific operator behaviors and notable built-in operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Many operators either mirror C or are specific to gp. Notable behaviors: postﬁx ++/-- are unary and return the new value (like C prefix ++); there is no preﬁx ++. Selection operator [ ] extracts components and can appear before assignment to assign to the selected component. ' (prime) performs derivative with respect to main variable (numeric derivative for closures). ~ is transpose. ! is both factorial (postfix) and logical not (prefix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware ++/-- are not associative (x++++ invalid). Use parentheses when in doubt. Some operators have different priorities vs C (<<,>>).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic and division operators semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators include * (multiplication), / (exact division producing rationals), \ and % (Euclidean quotient and remainder), \/ (rounded Euclidean quotient), and <<,>> (binary shifts defined as multiplication/division by powers of 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For polynomials deg r < deg y for x\y and x%y. Right shift defined as x>>n = x<<(-n). Prefer shift operators to multiplication where efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical operators and short-circuit evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical && and || evaluate left to right and short-circuit as soon as final truth value is known (second operand not evaluated if not needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to avoid errors (e.g., x == 0 || test(1/x) will not evaluate test(1/x) when x == 0). Combine type checks with && to avoid invalid calls (type(p) == 't_INT' && isprime(p)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment = versus equality test == and identity ===
rubrics_metrics.description: = is assignment and returns the value assigned; == tests exact equality (coercions may treat different zero-like objects equal); === tests component-wise identity (stricter than ==).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment is right-associative and requires an lvalue on left. Use op= (e.g., +=, *=) frequently for legibility and slight efficiency. Examples: x = 'x; x += x *= 2 -> 3*x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of composed assignment operators (op=) and ++/-- for clarity and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer using op= (lvalue op= expr) and ++/-- where possible because they are more legible and slightly more efficient than repeating expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: v[i+j-1]++ is clearer and faster than v[i+j-1] = v[i+j-1] + 1. Benchmarks show small time savings for loops. Shift operators also more efficient than multiply by two in large exponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable names and reserved identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid variable name starts with a letter followed by keyword or alphanumeric characters ([A-Za-z0-9]). Built-in function names and constants (Pi, Euler, Catalan, I, oo) are reserved. GP names are case-sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can use up to 16383 variable names (65535 on 64-bit). If you need thousands of variables, prefer vectors (X[1], X[2], ...) over many separate names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote operator 't registers free variables and unbound variable caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The quote operator 't registers a new free variable (monomial) t. For backward compatibility, using a variable name for the first time without assignment is interpreted as 't rather than raising an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: don't rely on the implicit creation of free variables in serious programs; explicitly do t = 't or use 't directly. Examples show how subst and eval interact with quoted and unquoted variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable priority ordering for multivariate polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables are implicitly ordered (priority) by the interpreter; the highest priority variable becomes the main variable in a stored multivariate polynomial, affecting internal representation and computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To control ordering, register variables in desired order at session start (e.g., 'x; 'y; 'z;). Use varhigher/varlower to create new variables with specific priorities. Beware: variable ordering affects Euclidean division and content/denominator computations in subtle ways (examples show x/y vs y/x differences).
